claim: On 2026-11-18 nine PDFs were downloaded, turned to text with pdftotext and read: Yu 2014, Harding 2017, Agrawal 1987, Silo 2013, Larson 2011, Kung and Robinson 1981, Calvin 2012, Gray 1976 and Ports and Grittner 2012.
The word escalation does not occur in the Gray et al. 1976 granularity paper (searched).
The Calvin 2012 paper does not say whether it supports interactive transactions (searched, no match).
The Gray et al. 1976 paper has no lock-count measurement; it is an argument and a protocol.
The Yu et al. 2014 text states no absolute throughput; the numbers are only in its figures, which were not read as numbers.
The Silo 2013 paper has no direct two-phase-locking versus OCC curve under heavy write contention; its contended test is against partition locks.
Six works were not read (Cahill 2008, Diaconu 2013, Berenson 1995, Thomas 1979, O'Neil 1986, Mohan); their rows are summary or textbook only.
The Gray et al. 1976 granularity paper was read in full as an OCR scan with spacing errors, 2371 lines.
Kung and Robinson 1981 was read in full as plain text of 230 lines.
Yu et al. 2014 was read in full as pdftotext plain text; the -layout copy is two-column and unreadable.
Harding et al. 2017 was read in full as plain text.
Agrawal, Carey and Livny 1987 was read in full as plain text.
Silo 2013 was read in full as plain text.
Larson et al. 2012 (arXiv 1201.0228) was read in full as plain text.
Calvin 2012 was read in full as plain text of 349 lines.
Ports and Grittner 2012 was read in full and stands in for Cahill 2008 in the snapshot-isolation and SSI rows.
Two-phase locking and its serializability are known only as textbook knowledge; no URL was fetched.
Multigranularity locking's serializability is textbook knowledge with no URL fetched; only the Gray et al. 1976 quotes were read.
The deadlock-prevention guarantees (wait-die and wound-wait deadlock-free and starvation-free) are textbook; their measures are quoted from Yu 2014 and Harding 2017.
Timestamp ordering and the Thomas write rule are textbook knowledge; their measures are quoted from Yu 2014 and Harding 2017 only.
The MVCC guarantee that read-only transactions never block or abort is textbook; its measures are quoted from Yu 2014, Harding 2017 and Larson 2012.
The snapshot-isolation guarantee and its ANSI-anomaly reading rest on a summary of Berenson et al. 1995, which was not read; the write-skew example is quoted from Ports and Grittner 2012.
The Cahill et al. 2008 SSI figures (SmallBank, InnoDB, Berkeley DB) are summary only and not read; the SSI serializability theorem is textbook.
Calvin's ordering-before-execution mechanism is textbook knowledge that the paper's 10-millisecond epoch quote confirms.
Predicate locks and next-key locking are textbook knowledge with no URL fetched; the figure for next-key locking is not recalled.
Escrow transactions are textbook knowledge with no URL fetched.
The papers disagree on one optimistic-versus-locking crossover: Yu and Harding report OCC better under skew, while Agrawal and Yu at medium contention report locking better.

claim: Gray et al. 1976: a fine lockable unit raises concurrency but a complex transaction setting many locks pays set-and-reset and storage overhead, while a coarse unit discriminates against transactions that want one record.
Gray et al. 1976: a node is locked in S or X only after all its ancestors are tagged in intention mode, and intention modes are compatible with one another.
Kung and Robinson 1981 define optimistic control as a read phase on local copies, a validation phase and a possible write phase.
Kung and Robinson 1981 say the simplest implementation puts transaction numbering, validation and the write phase in one critical section.
Kung and Robinson 1981: the major difficulty of locking is deadlock, solved by backup; the major difficulty of optimistic control is starvation, solved by locking.
Kung and Robinson 1981 say optimistic methods may be superior to locking where transaction conflict is highly unlikely, such as query-dominant systems and very large tree-structured indexes.
Kung and Robinson 1981 state that techniques are definitely needed for determining all instances where an optimistic approach is better than locking.
Kung and Robinson 1981 estimate, for d=3, m=199 and n=10^4, a restart probability pc below 0.0007 for B-tree insertions; this is an analytic bound, not a measurement.
Kung and Robinson 1981 give, for each pair with t(i) less than t(j), three validation conditions, the first being that Ti completes its write phase before Tj starts its read phase.
Yu et al. 2014 (simulated up to 1024 cores): all algorithms fail to scale to this magnitude, but for different reasons.
Yu et al. 2014 name five scalability bottlenecks: lock thrashing, preemptive aborts, deadlocks, timestamp allocation and memory-to-memory copying.
Yu et al. 2014, fixed-order 2PL: throughput scales almost linearly at theta=0, peaks at several hundred cores then thrashes at theta=0.6, and peaks at 16 cores at theta=0.8.
Yu et al. 2014 at theta=0.6: NO_WAIT and WAIT_DIE are the only 2PL schemes that scale past 512 cores, NO_WAIT better than WAIT_DIE.
Yu et al. 2014 at theta=0.6: DL_DETECT is inhibited by lock thrashing at 256 cores.
Yu et al. 2014 at theta=0.6: OCC does not perform as well because it spends a large portion of its time aborting transactions.
Yu et al. 2014 at theta=0.8: almost all schemes cannot scale beyond 64 cores, and NO_WAIT leads at first then succumbs to lock thrashing.
Yu et al. 2014 at theta=0.8 on 1024 cores: OCC performs the best, because one transaction is always allowed to commit.
Yu et al. 2014 at 64 cores: contention has little effect for theta below 0.6, then a sudden throughput drop that approaches zero above 0.8.
Yu et al. 2014 at 512 cores with short transactions: DL_DETECT and NO_WAIT perform best, and OCC performs worst because it allocates double the timestamps.
Yu et al. 2014 at 64 cores, theta=0.8: MVCC has the best performance with few write transactions; TIMESTAMP and OCC perform poorly because they copy tuples for reads.
Yu et al. 2014: H-STORE outperforms all other schemes up to 800 cores, for single-partition transactions with uniform access only.
Yu et al. 2014: the DBMS does not scale with transactions accessing four or more partitions, in a run with 10 percent multi-partition transactions at 1024 cores.
Yu et al. 2014, TPC-C with 4 warehouses: all schemes fail to scale when warehouses are fewer than cores; NewOrder scales up to 64 cores.
Yu et al. 2014, read-only workload: TIMESTAMP and OCC have significantly worse performance than the other algorithms regardless of core count, because they copy tuples to perform a read.
Harding et al. 2017, 16 servers: protocol throughput is relatively unaffected by skew up to theta 0.5; at theta 0.8 all but one converge to the same low performance, and CALVIN alone holds.
Harding et al. 2017: OCC performs worse than the other non-deterministic protocols under low contention, but at higher contention tolerating more conflicts outweighs its overheads.
Harding et al. 2017 at theta 0.6 with 100 percent update transactions: MVCC and TIMESTAMP perform at 33 percent of the throughput of NO_WAIT.
Harding et al. 2017 at theta 0.6 with 100 percent updates: NO_WAIT performs 54 percent better than the next-best non-deterministic algorithm, OCC.
Harding et al. 2017: at a 10 percent update rate there is an average of 1.4 aborts per transaction (WAIT_DIE).
Harding et al. 2017 conclude that with few updates a 2PL or timestamp protocol made most sense, and past a certain write threshold an optimistic or deterministic protocol was better.
Harding et al. 2017: OCC is slightly more resilient to high skew, but once skew reaches a critical point CALVIN is the most consistent protocol.
Harding et al. 2017: except CALVIN, throughput plummets when transactions touch more than one partition; from two to four partitions performance drops 12-40 percent.
Harding et al. 2017: at 64 servers the protocols improve single-server performance 1.7-3.8x, and NO_WAIT has the best overall performance at all server counts.
Harding et al. 2017: CALVIN throughput fell 36 percent on 16 servers at medium contention (theta 0.6, 50 percent updates) with data-dependent aborts.
Harding et al. 2017: with data-dependent aborts CALVIN throughput declines from 73k to 19k transactions per second as theta goes from 0.8 to 0.9.
Harding et al. 2017 on PPS: CALVIN is flat-lined at about 7k transactions per second because of reconnaissance queries, and OCC's abort rate of 15 percent is as high as NO_WAIT's.
Harding et al. 2017: distributed transactions on a cluster often exceed single-machine throughput only by small amounts.
Silo 2013 reports almost 700,000 transactions per second on a standard TPC-C mix on a 32-core machine, with near-linear scalability.
Silo 2013: per-core throughput at 32 cores is 91 percent of that at 8 cores, and a commercial main-memory system does at most 3,000 transactions per second per core on the authors' hardware.
Silo 2013 assumes a one-shot request model; the paper says client communication inside a transaction would grow the likelihood of abort.
Silo 2013: MemSilo+GlobalTID shows a scalability collapse after 24 workers, and Key-Value outperforms it by 1.80x at 32 workers.
Silo 2013: Key-Value outperforms MemSilo by a maximum of 1.07x, the overhead of read and write tracking.

Silo 2013: Partitioned-Store outperforms MemSilo by 1.54x with no cross-partition transactions, falls below MemSilo at roughly 20 percent cross-partition, and MemSilo outperforms it by 2.98x at roughly 60 percent.
Silo 2013 with one hot counter per district: MemSilo outperforms Partitioned-Store by a maximum of 8.20x at 24 workers, and 17.21x at 32 workers with the counter taken out of the transaction.
Silo 2013: MemSilo outperforms MemSilo+NoSS by 1.19x because large read-only transactions abort under concurrent modification; snapshots cost a 3.4 percent memory increase.
Agrawal, Carey and Livny 1987 (simulation): dynamic two-phase locking outperforms immediate-restart and optimistic control at medium to high resource utilization.
Agrawal et al. 1987: when utilization is low and many transactions are available, the optimistic algorithm performs best of the three.
Agrawal et al. 1987 with 5 and 10 resource units: blocking gives the highest overall throughput, with maximum useful disk utilization of 72 percent at 5 units and 56 percent at 10 units.
Agrawal et al. 1987 with 25 resource units: the optimistic maximum throughput beats blocking's, although not by very much.
Agrawal et al. 1987 with 50 resource units: maximum useful utilizations are down in the range of 15 to 25 percent.
Agrawal et al. 1987 interactive runs with one resource unit and think times of 1, 5 and 10 s: the optimistic algorithm provided the best performance.
Agrawal et al. 1987: under low resource contention and high multiprogramming, blocking may start thrashing before restarts do.
Agrawal et al. 1987 say it is an open question whether such low utilizations occur in real systems, and that the proper algorithm choice is strongly resource dependent.
Agrawal et al. 1987: if the multiprogramming level rises beyond a certain level, blocking and optimistic control start thrashing.

Larson et al. 2012: single-version locking performs well when transactions are short and contention is low but degrades under demanding conditions, while multiversion schemes are much less sensitive to hotspots and long-running transactions.
Larson et al. 2012 at low contention (10M rows, 10 reads and 2 writes): single-version locking reaches over 2M transactions per second and MV/L is 30 percent lower than MV/O.
Larson et al. 2012 with a 1,000-row hotspot: all schemes exceed a million transactions per second, with MV/O slightly ahead of both locking schemes.

Larson et al. 2012 at 24 threads: Repeatable Read costs under 2 percent for both locking schemes, MV/O's repeated reads cost 8 percent, and serializability costs 10%-19% lower throughput for both MV schemes.
Larson et al. 2012 with 80 percent read-only transactions on the 1,000-row table: the MVCC schemes achieve 63 percent and 73 percent higher throughput than 1V.
Larson et al. 2012 with long readers each reading 10 percent of a 10M-row table, at x=1: update throughput drops 75 percent for single-version locking and 5 percent for the MV schemes.
Larson et al. 2012: when 50 percent of active transactions are long readers, at x=12, MV has 80X higher update throughput than 1V.
Larson et al. 2012: the optimistic MVCC scheme consistently achieves higher throughput than the pessimistic multiversion scheme.
Larson et al. 2012 say whether Cahill et al.'s SSI approach can be implemented efficiently in a main-memory DBMS is an open question.

Ports and Grittner 2012 (PostgreSQL 9.1): serializable mode has a performance cost of less than 7 percent relative to snapshot isolation and outperforms two-phase locking significantly on some workloads.
Ports and Grittner 2012: tracking read dependencies has a CPU overhead of 10-20 percent on a simple benchmark.
Ports and Grittner 2012: in the in-memory configuration SSI causes a 5 percent slowdown relative to snapshot isolation, from increased CPU use.
Ports and Grittner 2012: SSI outperforms strict two-phase locking for all transaction mixes, by a larger margin when the read-only fraction is high.
Ports and Grittner 2012: on the disk-bound 150-warehouse run SSI is indistinguishable from SI, and the serialization failure rate was under 0.25 percent.
Ports and Grittner 2012: two transactions that read the same data and modify disjoint sets give write skew under snapshot isolation, and write locks do not solve it.
Ports and Grittner 2012: SSI checks for a dangerous structure of two adjacent rw-antidependency edges, which may give false positives because not every such structure is part of a cycle.
Thomson et al. 2012 (Calvin): time is divided into 10-millisecond epochs, during which each machine's sequencer collects transaction requests.
Thomson et al. 2012 (Calvin): around 5000 New Order transactions per second per node in clusters larger than 10 nodes, and nearly half a million per second on a 100-node cluster.
Thomson et al. 2012: Calvin does not natively support dependent transactions, because its deterministic locking needs every read and write set in advance.

Thomson et al. 2012 microbenchmark: under low contention Calvin gets the same approximately 5x to 7x per-node slowdown going from 1 machine to 4 or 8 machines (27000 to about 5000 or 4000 transactions per second).
Thomson et al. 2012 give a model, not a measurement, of a two-phase-commit comparison, assuming locks held about 8 ms per distributed transaction, as a strong lower bound on slowdown.
Thomson et al. 2012: ping times between replicas were 100 ms to 170 ms and total throughput was not affected by the replication mode; latency figures were not read.
Cahill et al. 2008 was not opened: dl.acm.org gave HTTP 403, the Washington copy a login page, core.ac.uk an error page and the usyd repository no file, so its SmallBank figures are unknown.
Diaconu et al. 2013 (Hekaton in SQL Server) was not obtained.
Berenson et al. 1995 was not read, so the snapshot-isolation row stays summary.
Eswaran 1976, Rosenkrantz 1978, Thomas 1979, O'Neil 1986 and Mohan (ARIES/KVL) were not read, and no search was run for them.
Figures inside charts (throughput per core count in Yu, Harding, Agrawal and Larson) were not read; only sentences from the text are quoted.
The Calvin 2012 latency numbers in its Figure 2 were not read.
The SSI row's claim that InnoDB gives fewer false positives than Berkeley DB comes from a forum relay and was not checked.
The first-pass row said Yu et al. 2014's best 2PL spends about 30 percent of cycles on useful work; the paper text has no such figure.
